etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English triangle, from Old French triangle, from Latin triangulum, noun use of adjective triangulus (“three-cornered, having three angles”), from trēs (“three”) + angulus (“corner, angle”), equivalent to tri- +‎ angle.

definitions.definition: (geometry) A polygon with three sides and three angles.

quote.citation: 1981, William Irwin Thompson, The Time Falling Bodies Take to Light: Mythology, Sexuality and the Origins of Culture, London: Rider/Hutchinson & Co., page 22:
quote.text: The wedge-shaped character was the triangle, the archaic Paleolithic sign of the vulva; the pubic triangle was at the end of the phallic stylus.

definitions.definition: (music) A percussion instrument made by forming a metal rod into a triangular shape which is open at one angle. It is suspended from a string and hit with a metal bar to make a resonant sound.
(cue sports) A triangular piece of equipment used for gathering the balls into the formation required by the game being played.

quote.citation: 2009, Neil McDonald, Quadrant, November 2009, No. 461 (Volume LIII, Number 11), Quadrant Magazine Limited, page 104:
quote.text: One of the writers' most pleasing inventions was to treat the triangle love story as comedy.

definitions.definition: (systemics) The structure of systems composed with three interrelated objects.
A draughtsman's square in the form of a right-angled triangle.
(historical, usually in the plural) A frame formed of three poles stuck in the ground and united at the top, to which people were bound when undergoing corporal punishment.

quote.citation: 1868, “The Week”, in The Nation‎[1], volume 6, number 149:
quote.text: But nothing is said as to what we are to do with the negro when we have cut him off from absolute dominion; we are not informed if we may spread him on the triangles as aforetime;

definitions.definition: Any of various large papilionid butterflies of the genus Graphium.
(rail transport) A triangular formation of railway tracks, with a curve on at least one side.

quote.citation: 1961 March, ""Balmore"", “Driving and firing modern French steam locomotives”, in Trains Illustrated, page 147:
quote.text: After turning on the triangle at Jeumont, we set off light engine back to Aulnoye.
